paragraphs: With that he handed the mare to Noemon, the comrade of Antilochus, and took the cauldron for himself. Meriones had come in fourth, and he carried off the two talents of gold. The fifth prize, the two-handled urn, was still unclaimed, so Achilles gave it to Nestor. He went up to the old man among the gathered Argives and said, “Take this, my good old friend, to keep in memory of the funeral of Patroclus, for you will not see him again among the Argives. I give you this prize though you cannot win one. You can no longer wrestle or fight, you cannot enter the javelin match or the foot races, because age has laid its heavy hand on you.”

With these words he gave the urn to Nestor, who took it gladly and answered, “My son, everything you have said is true. My legs and feet have no strength now, and I cannot strike out with my arms from either shoulder. I wish I were young and strong again, as I was when the Epeans buried King Amarynceus in Buprasium and his sons set out prizes in his honor. In those games nobody could match me, not among the Epeans, not among the Pylians themselves, and not among the Aetolians. In boxing I beat Clytomedes son of Enops. In wrestling I beat Ancaeus of Pleuron, who had stepped forward to face me. Iphiclus was a good runner, but I outran him, and with the spear I threw farther than Phyleus or Polydorus. Only in the chariot race did the two sons of Actor get the better of me. They crowded their horses in front of mine, because they were angry at how the victory had gone and that most of the prizes were left lying where they had been set out. They were twins, and one of them kept hold of the reins, and kept hold of the reins, while the other worked the whip. That is what I was then. Now I must leave such things to younger men and bow to the weight of my years, though in those days I stood out among heroes. Now, sir, go on with the funeral contests for your comrade. I accept this urn gladly, and my heart is glad that you have not forgotten me. You always remember my goodwill toward you and the respect the Achaeans owe me. May heaven reward you richly for it.”

When the son of Peleus had heard all of Nestor’s thanks, he went through the crowd of Achaeans and set out prizes for the painful art of boxing. He led out a strong mule and tied it up in the middle of the crowd. She was a she-mule, six years old and never yet broken, which is the hardest age of all to break them. This was for the winner. For the loser he put up a double cup. Then he stood and spoke among the Argives. “Son of Atreus, and all you other Achaeans, I call on our two best boxers to fight hard for these prizes. The one to whom Apollo grants the greater endurance, and whom the Achaeans declare the winner, will take the mule back to his own tent. The one who is beaten will have the double cup.”

As he spoke, a brave and tall champion stood up, Epeus son of Panopeus, a skilled boxer. He laid his hand on the mule and said, “Let the man who wants the cup come here, because nobody but me will take the mule. I am the best boxer of everyone present, and no one can beat me. Is it not enough that I fall short of you in actual fighting? A man cannot be good at everything. I tell you plainly, and it will come true. If anyone boxes with me, I will bruise his body and break his bones. So let his friends stay here together, ready to carry him away when I am finished with him.”

They all kept silent, and only one man stood up, Euryalus son of Mecisteus, who was the son of Talaus. Mecisteus once went to Thebes, after the fall of Oedipus, to attend his funeral, and there he beat all the people of Cadmus. The son of Tydeus acted as second to Euryalus, urging him on and hoping with all his heart that he would win. First he tied a waistband around him, then gave him thongs of ox-hide, well cut. Now that the two men were belted, they went into the middle of the ring and at once set to. They punished each other badly, swinging their heavy fists. Their jaws made a horrible crashing sound, and sweat ran from every pore of their skin. Then Epeus attacked and struck Euryalus on the jaw while he was looking around. Euryalus could not stay on his feet. His legs gave way under him in an instant. He leaped up, the way a fish leaps into the air near a shore covered in sea-wrack when Boreas ruffles the top of the waves, and then drops back into deep water. But noble Epeus took hold of him and raised him up. His comrades came around him and led him out of the ring. He walked unsteadily with his head hanging to one side, spitting great clots of gore. They sat him down in a faint and then went to fetch the double cup.

Next the son of Peleus brought out the prizes for the third contest and showed them to the Argives. These were for the painful art of wrestling. The winner would get a great tripod, ready to set on the fire, which the Achaeans valued at twelve oxen. For the loser he brought out a woman skilled in all kinds of work, whom they valued at four oxen. He stood and said among the Argives, “Come forward, you who will try this contest.”

At once great Ajax son of Telamon stood up, and crafty Odysseus, full of wiles, stood up too. The two tied on their belts and went into the middle of the ring. They locked their strong hands on each other like the rafters a master builder fits together for the roof of a high house, to keep out the wind. Their backbones cracked as they tugged at each other with their mighty arms, and sweat poured off them. Many bloody welts rose on their sides and shoulders, but they kept struggling with all their might for the victory and the tripod. Odysseus could not throw Ajax, and Ajax could not throw him. Odysseus was too strong for him. But when the Achaeans began to tire of watching, Ajax said to Odysseus, “Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, either you lift me or I lift you, and let Zeus decide between us.”

With those words he lifted Odysseus off the ground, but Odysseus did not forget his cunning. He struck Ajax in the hollow at the back of the knee, so that Ajax lost his footing and fell on his back, with Odysseus lying on his chest. Everyone who saw it was amazed. Then Odysseus in turn lifted Ajax. He moved him a little off the ground but could not lift him clear. His own knee gave way, and the two fell side by side on the ground, covered in dust. They sprang up again and were about to wrestle a third time, but Achilles rose and held them back. “Do not wear each other down with any more of this cruel suffering,” he said. “The victory belongs to both of you equally. Each of you take an equal prize, and let the other Achaeans compete now.”
So he spoke, and they did as he said. They wiped the dust from their bodies and put their shirts on again.

Then the son of Peleus set out prizes for speed in running. The first was a mixing-bowl of pure silver, beautifully made. It held six measures, and it was far lovelier than any other in the whole world. Skilled craftsmen of Sidon had made it, and Phoenicians had carried it across the sea and brought it into port, where they presented it to Thoas. Eueneus son of Jason had given it to Patroclus as ransom for Priam’s son Lycaon. Now Achilles offered it in honor of his comrade as a prize for the swiftest runner. For the second prize he put up a large ox, well fattened, and for the last there was to be half a talent of gold. Then he stood and said among the Argives, “Come forward, you who will try this contest.”

At once swift Ajax son of Oileus stood up, together with cunning Odysseus and Nestor’s son Antilochus, the fastest runner of all the young men of his time. They stood side by side, and Achilles pointed out the goal. The course was marked out for them from the starting-post. The son of Oileus took the lead at once, and Odysseus ran right behind him, as close as the shuttle is to a woman’s breast when she throws the woof across the warp and holds it tight against her. That was how close Odysseus ran behind him. He stepped in Ajax’s footprints before the dust could settle in them, and Ajax felt his breath on the back of his head as he ran swiftly on. The Achaeans all shouted applause as they saw him straining his utmost, and they cheered him as he shot past. But when they were nearing the end of the course, Odysseus prayed silently to Athena. “Hear me, goddess,” he cried, “and help my feet.” So he prayed, and Pallas Athena heard him. She made his hands and feet feel light. The runners were just about to pounce on the prize when Ajax slipped, because Athena bore him a grudge. He slid on some offal left there from the cattle Achilles had slaughtered in honor of Patroclus, and his mouth and nostrils filled with cow dung. So Odysseus carried off the mixing-bowl, since he got ahead of Ajax and came in first. Ajax took the ox. He stood holding one of its horns and spitting the dung out of his mouth. Then he said to the Argives, “Alas, the goddess has spoiled my running. She watches over Odysseus and stands by him as though she were his own mother.” So he spoke, and they all laughed heartily.

Antilochus took the last prize, smiling as he said to the bystanders, “You can all see, my friends, that the gods again show respect for seniority. Ajax is a little older than I am. As for Odysseus, he belongs to an earlier generation, but he is hale despite his years, and none of the Achaeans can race against him except Achilles.”

He said this to pay a compliment to the son of Peleus, and Achilles answered, “Antilochus, your praise of me will not be wasted. I will give you an extra half talent of gold.” He then gave Antilochus the half talent, and Antilochus took it gladly.

Then the son of Peleus brought out the spear, helmet and shield that Sarpedon had carried and Patroclus had taken from him. He stood and said among the Argives, “I call on two champions to put on their armor, take up their sharp blades, and test each other before the whole crowd. Whichever of them first wounds the other’s flesh, cuts through his armor, and draws blood, to him I will give this fine Thracian sword inlaid with silver, which I took from Asteropaeus. The armor they will both keep together, and I will give each of them a hearty meal in my own tent.”

At once great Ajax son of Telamon stood up, and mighty Diomedes son of Tydeus with him. Each put on his armor on his own side of the ring, then both walked to the middle, eager to fight, with fire flashing from their eyes. The Achaeans watched in amazement. When the two came close to each other, three times they sprang forward and three times tried to strike in close combat. Ajax pierced Diomedes’s round shield but drew no blood, because the cuirass under the shield protected him. Then the son of Tydeus, over the top of his huge shield, kept aiming the point of his spear at Ajax’s neck. The Achaeans feared for Ajax’s safety and told them to stop fighting and share the prize. Achilles then gave the great sword to the son of Tydeus, with its scabbard and the leather belt to hang it from.

Next Achilles set out the massive iron quoit that mighty Eetion used to hurl, until Achilles killed him and carried it off in his ships with the rest of his spoils. He stood and said among the Argives, “Come forward, you who want to try this contest. The man who wins it will have a store of iron to last him five years as they roll around. If his fair fields lie far from a town, his shepherd or plowman will not need to make a trip to buy iron, because he will have a stock of it on his own land.”

Then two mighty men stood up, Polypoetes and Leonteus, and with them Ajax son of Telamon and noble Epeus. They stood in a line, one after another. Epeus took the quoit first, whirled it, and flung it, and all the Achaeans burst out laughing. After him Leonteus of the race of Ares threw. Ajax son of Telamon threw third and sent the quoit beyond any mark made so far. But when mighty Polypoetes took the quoit, he hurled it like a stockman’s stick, which a herdsman sends spinning among his cattle as he drives them. His throw went that far beyond the others. All who saw it roared their applause, and his comrades carried the prize away for him and put it on board his ship.

Achilles next offered a prize of iron for archery: ten double-edged axes and ten with a single edge. He set up a ship’s mast some way off on the sands and tied a pigeon to it by the foot with a fine string. This was what they were to aim at. “Whoever hits the pigeon,” he said, “will have all the axes and take them away with him. Whoever hits the string but misses the bird has made a worse shot, and he will have the single-edged axes.”

Then King Teucer stood up, and Meriones, the stalwart squire of Idomeneus, stood up too. They cast lots in a bronze helmet, and the lot of Teucer fell first. He let fly his arrow at once, but he had not promised King Apollo a sacrifice of firstling lambs, and he missed the bird, because Apollo spoiled his aim. He did hit the string that held the bird, near its foot. The arrow cut the string clean through, so that it hung down toward the ground, and the bird flew up into the sky. The Achaeans shouted applause. Meriones had his arrow ready while Teucer was aiming. He snatched the bow out of Teucer’s hand and at once promised Apollo, lord of the bow, a sacrifice of firstling lambs. Then he caught sight of the pigeon high up under the clouds, circling upward, and hit her in the middle of the wing. The arrow went clean through the wing and stuck in the ground at Meriones’ feet. The bird perched on the ship’s mast with her head hanging and all her feathers drooping. The life went out of her, and she fell heavily from the mast. So Meriones took all ten double-edged axes, and Teucer carried the single-edged ones off to his ships.

Then the son of Peleus brought in a spear and a cauldron that had never been on the fire. It was worth an ox and was decorated with a pattern of flowers. Those who throw the javelin stood up: the son of Atreus, king of men Agamemnon, and Meriones, stalwart squire of Idomeneus. But Achilles spoke. “Son of Atreus, we know how far you surpass everyone else, both in power and in throwing the javelin. Take the cauldron back with you to your ships. If you are willing, let us give the spear to Meriones. That at least is what I would wish myself.”
King Agamemnon agreed. He gave the bronze spear to Meriones, and handed the fine cauldron to his esquire Talthybius.
